hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text: The dirty little secret about magnesium supplements - 400 mg of magnesium citrate is not 400 mg of magnesium. Magnesium citrate contains both magnesium and citrate. A label listing only “magnesium citrate, 400 mg” gives the weight of the entire compound, not the elemental magnesium dose, and can make the dose look much larger than it is. A clear label should read something like: “Magnesium (as magnesium glycinate), 120 mg, 29% Daily Value.” Magnesium also has an established Daily Value. If the panel says otherwise, that’s another red flag, and a reason to check the labels on your other mineral supplements, too!

hits.text: Women who delivered very preterm had vitamin D levels about 25% lower than women who delivered at term. Average 25(OH)D was 26.2 ng/mL among births before 32 weeks, compared with 34.8 ng/mL at term. Women delivering between 32 and 36 weeks also had lower levels, averaging 31.3 ng/mL. hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text: The article “The Surprising Science of an All-Meat Diet,” which I published last week, is now on the most-read list for health articles and uptrending. This morning, I also finished an interview with a major newspaper in the United Kingdom that was interested in covering my perspective on saturated fat and cholesterol for National Cholesterol Month in the UK. A brief summary of my two major positions, because I don’t think they’re at all radical. I’ll be as concise as possible and link to more information below. 1) First, the carnivore diet is a tool, not a religion. It’s a mistake to present it as the best diet for humans or to make strong claims that go beyond the literature, such as that it will improve longevity. What we can say, accurately and humbly, is that it’s helping many people who have struggled with debilitating disorders and failed to find support through conventional approaches. We can also say that there is strong biological plausibility for many of the conditions for which it’s being used, including mental health disorders and autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. That’s not definitive proof. But it’s a possibility that deserves curiosity and compassion, not disdain. If you want the full scientific breakdown in video form: “The Strange Science of Eating Only Meat” youtu.be/WJnPDQ0XRXA 2) The second major point I’ll make is that CONTEXT matters. Meat is vilified largely because of its saturated fat and cholesterol content. However, when it comes to improving the cardiometabolic health of the general population, focusing on reducing saturated fat intake is like worrying about a mosquito when you’re being chased by a tiger. We now have randomized controlled trial data showing that low-carbohydrate ketogenic diets (despite typically being much higher in saturated fat and cholesterol) can provide greater improvements in many cardiometabolic risk markers than low-fat plant-based or Mediterranean-style diets higher in carbohydrates, particularly in people with obesity and insulin resistance. More here: staycuriousmetabolism.substack.com/p/a-major-tria … At the end of the day, I don’t fancy myself a carnivore fanboy. Just carnivore-curious and open-minded. That’s enough. P.S. There’s a tendency to make meat and diet unnecessarily political. Resist that tendency. What’s on my plate does not inform what I do at the ballot box. Stereotypes impair our ability to have thoughtful academic discourse. Ht/ @MikhailaFuller for her contribution (including the click-boost from her adorable baby) @EpochTimes

hits.text: Women with a history of menopausal hormone therapy had 2.5% greater grip strength at ages 60-64 than women who had never used it. Among women 80 and older, that gap was 14.3%. Activity patterns added an interesting layer. Among women 65 and older, those with a history of hormone therapy and intermediate amounts of moderate-intensity physical activity had 16% greater grip strength, while those who were the most sedentary still had 14% greater grip strength if they'd undergone hormone therapy vs. not. Menopausal hormone therapy may help preserve strength into later life, including among women who aren't very active. But of course, regular activity is crucial for strength preservation and should be done regardless of whether or not someone is on hormone therapy.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: Alcohol is a hot topic (and an odd one for a guy like me to bring up--I've never had a drop in my life). But there is a relevant metabolic angle to it. If you drink most nights while trying to lose fat, you are regularly shutting down fat oxidation. The body clears alcohol first--it's a fuel that demands "priority boarding". While that is happening, fat burning drops hard, and more of the fat from your meals gets stored instead of burned. In one study, subjects drank about 96 g of alcohol in a day (roughly seven drinks), and 24-hour fat burning fell by about a third. That drop showed up whether the alcohol was added on top of their meals or swapped in for other calories. If you're looking to lose fat, I'd put alcohol at the top of the list of things to scrutinize. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1545851/

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: I've been hearing people say glucose spikes don't matter as long as your average blood sugar looks fine. Your brain may disagree. Researchers put continuous glucose monitors on older adults for three days and then scanned their brains. The people whose glucose swung up and down the most over 30 minutes to 2 hours had less gray matter in the hippocampus (the brain's memory center) and did worse on cognitive tests. That held even after accounting for HbA1c (the three-month blood sugar average most doctors check). A normal average can hide plenty of spikes and crashes. I'd pay attention to what happens after meals, not just the number on your lab report. Ideally, keep the swings small. And really only a CGM can tell you this.
hits.draft_en:
“Average blood sugar looks fine” can still hide spikes that hit the memory centre.

Older adults with the wildest swings had less hippocampal gray matter and worse cognition — even when HbA1c looked okay.

After meals matter. Walk ten minutes. Don’t wash lunch down with soft drink. Ask about a CGM if you’re guessing.
hits.video_tip: 25–35s post-lunch walk; caption “spikes hide in a ‘fine’ average.”

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text: If you're a young woman with insulin resistance, your brain may already be burning fuel like a 70-year-old's. Lean women in their 20s with PCOS/PMOS (polycystic ovary syndrome; a hormonal condition driven largely by insulin resistance, and one of the most common hormone disorders in women) had brains taking up 9 to 14% less glucose than women of the same age and weight. In healthy 70-year-olds, the same lab found drops of about 8 to 17%. The more insulin resistant a woman was, the less fuel her brain took in, and the pattern looked like early Alzheimer's disease. And it showed! Five of the seven scored low on memory tests. None were impaired yet, but these were women in their 20s. That matters because women already carry more of the Alzheimer's burden, making up nearly two-thirds of Americans living with it. Insulin resistance is one reason, and it can start decades earlier than anyone looks. None of these women were overweight, and their fasting blood sugar was close to normal. Their insulin told the real story. Ladies, if your doctor only checks glucose, ask for fasting insulin.

outsiders.name: Anthropic
outsiders.text: What do you want from AI? We’re launching a new study with Anthropic Interviewer to learn more about your experiences using AI, what role you want it to play in your life and the world, and what you want from the companies building it. Last December, 81,000 people told us about their hopes and fears about AI in the largest qualitative study ever done. This time, we’re giving participants the option to make their responses public so that anyone, not just Anthropic, can learn from them. What you tell us will shape The Anthropic Institute’s research and inform the decisions we make. If many people say companies like Anthropic should be doing something differently, that will be on the record, where anyone can point to it. The study runs Sept 29 to Oct 6 and is open to Free, Pro, and Max users on Claude and Claude Code. Take part here:

outsiders.text: GPT-6.1 Sol shows major improvements over GPT-6 Sol in our alignment evaluations, bringing it more in line with GPT-6 Astra. It’s more transparent about its limitations and more reliable at respecting user intent and safety constraints.

outsiders.name: Rodev
outsiders.text: Claude Code is a mess. Until you install this. There's an official Anthropic plugin called claude-code-setup. It tells you what automations you can set up (hooks, skills, MCP servers, subagents…) and how to configure them step by step. Basically, it analyzes your project and recommends what to activate. To install it: /plugin install claude-code-setup@claude-plugins-official Save this post so you don't lose it 🔖

outsiders.name: Claude
outsiders.text: @LEJ_limited gave Sonnet 5.5 a 60×46 pixel emoji and asked for a 3D model he could print. A few hours later, it was on his desk.

outsiders.name: Alex Finn
outsiders.text: OpenAI just released Dots, their competitor to Grok Bot and Muse I've had early access for a bit, and I really like it Its biggest differentiators are that it has access to ALL your ChatGPT memories, as well as all the amazing tools in the ChatGPT harness including: • Voice mode • ChatGPT plugins • The new ChatGPT Spaces • much more Is it wildly differentiated from the other agents? No. But if you've been using ChatGPT for a while, the fact that it just knows you and all your past chats really well is massive And if you are a desktop app power user like me, being able to have your agent spin up codex threads on the go is wildly helpful If you are more in the 'normie' crowd who primarily just has your agent make restaurant reservations, probably not for you But if you use AI daily for more advanced stuff like building and doing all your knowledge work, it's excellent

outsiders.text: cancel me for this but...Claude Sonnet 5.5 + SEO is going to quietly create a bunch of business “mini millionaires” this year. don’t bookmark this if it crosses your timeline. Just paste this entire thing into Claude. It will change your life.

outsiders.name: Bober_smart
outsiders.text: It blows my mind how few people have implemented this setup. A year ago, this exact system allowed me to automate 90% of my tasks and expand my business Andrey Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI, dropped a simple idea that generated 22 million views and 108,000 saves "stop relying on AI strictly for generating code, and start leveraging it to build a personal second brain" The logic is straightforward: You link Claude Code to a specific directory and throw in any reference materials (articles, meeting transcripts, or PDFs) The system analyzes the text, maps out connections, and constructs a living repository of everything you know. It compounds continuously: as you feed it more data, the entire ecosystem becomes significantly smarter How it breaks down in practice: Launch Obsidian, set up a new repository, and connect it to Claude Code Feed in the template based on Karpathy's wiki approach and instruct Claude to deploy the architecture The model automatically constructs three core areas: raw for your incoming documents, wiki for organized pages, and a master CLAUDE file that coordinates all processes Move any new resource into the raw folder and issue a quick command to process it Query your entire personal knowledge base whenever you need answers A quick five-minute deployment means you will never have to initiate a prompt from a blank canvas again I published the complete guide in the article. Make sure to bookmark it for later
